en: The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, in one fascicle, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi people during the Southern Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].
There was an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, there was a prominent and wealthy family in Rājagṛha named Śoṇa.
Shenri had a son named Jianluo Fa (in the Han language, "Moonlight"), who possessed pure and clean conduct; because the Buddha compared him to a young boy, he was called Moonlight.
The youth Candraprabha went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha:

"Whether a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains at home or becomes a bhikṣu, he should practice the gift of Dharma and the gift of food, always welcoming the hearts of all people with a benevolent mind, and uphold the four vows regarding food. He should resolve his mind to seek Buddhahood and will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
What are the four vows?
The first vow is: may all people swiftly attain skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
The second vow is: may I, in every lifetime, meet with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The third vow is: may I share my wealth and treasures with all people;
the fourth vow is: may I practice two things—giving the Dharma and providing food—and may I always delight in attaining such conduct.
These are the four vows. "Furthermore, Candraprabha Kumāra!

Whether a bodhisattva mahāsattva is living at home or has gone forth from the home life, they should always delight in the gift of the Dharma; they should always welcome others with skillful means; their minds should be free from greed; they should abide correctly within the established Dharma; and they should reverently uphold the prohibitions and precepts in accordance with the Dharma."
Furthermore, Candraprabha Kumāra, there is another matter:
if a bhikṣu is afflicted by illness or in dire straits, one should diligently provide for his relief and grant him medicine;
and why stop at medicine?
Furthermore, one should not begrudge even one's own flesh and blood, but should provide for them so that they may recover.
"There is yet another matter, Youthful Moon-Bright!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has completed an act of giving, he must never harbor doubt."

Why is this? In the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—indeed, beyond all calculation, immeasurable, and infinitely vast and remote—there was a Buddha in the world named Tienian-yuan-wushangwang (Dhṛtimatipraṇidhānānuttararāja) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He manifested the reception of a body in the world, practicing and cultivating according to his inclinations, and served as the Most Honored One.
"Furthermore, Candraprabha, there was another matter:
at that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha King of Unsurpassed Vows (Anuttaravajrarāja) was clearly mindful;
on the very day he manifested the marks of a Samyaksaṃbuddha, he immediately transformed himself into countless bodies, according to [the needs of] those..."
With joy and delight, he guides them, causing countless people to attain the stage of *srotāpanna*,
countless people to attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, countless people to attain the stage of *anāgāmin*, countless people to attain the stage of *arhat*,
countless people to attain the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, and countless people to be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Above, countless people were born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; countless people were born in the Yāma Heaven; countless people were born in the Tuṣita Heaven;
countless people were born in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; countless people were born in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
countless people were born in the Brahmā Heaven; and countless people received individual predictions of their future enlightenment.
Regarding the aspiration for the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path, every person shall transcend through the Great Path of Nirvana.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha King of Aspiration for the Unsurpassed, dwelling in profound contemplation, gave this instruction and manifested his body for one day.
Once all those to be saved have been delivered, he will enter parinirvāṇa;
after his parinirvāṇa, his Dharma shall remain for twenty billion years.

When that number is nearly exhausted, during the final fifty years, many bhikṣus will no longer believe in the profound sūtras and will take pleasure in superficial matters; thus, the sūtra-Dharma will gradually come to an end.
"At that time, in the land of Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Jñānabala who constantly practiced three matters of the Buddha.
What are these three?
First, he always protected the profound Dharma of the Buddha;..."
Second, to receive and practice the profound Dharma of the Buddha;
third, to believe with certainty in the profound Dharma of the Buddha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the world named P'u-t'an-mo (in the Han language, "Ultimate Sincerity"), who constantly practiced these three things.
What are these three matters?
First, to constantly maintain this samādhi;
second, to constantly protect this samādhi; [and third, to constantly practice this samādhi].
Third, one should constantly recite this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are eight matters:

one should constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness, constantly practice a mind of compassion, constantly practice a mind of pity, constantly practice a mind of protection, constantly practice a mind of discerning wisdom, constantly practice a mind of responding to questions, constantly practice a mind of joyful exultation, and constantly practice the foremost mind.
By this, he was able to fully subdue the ninety-six types of heterodox paths; he comprehensively examined and understood each profound dharma without further doubt.
The bhikṣu Tohicitta (Zhichengyi) was related to King Jñānabala by kinship, and was thus respected by the king; the people of the country held him in high esteem as well.
The king never grew weary of wishing to see this bhikṣu;
he was never satiated by listening to this bhikṣu preach the Dharma;
and he was never satiated by wishing to pay homage to this bhikṣu.

At that time, a large and malignant ulcer broke out on the monk’s thigh; it could not be cured by the physicians or medicines of the kingdom, and the King was so overcome with grief that tears immediately flowed from his eyes.
At that moment, twenty thousand ladies-in-waiting likewise simultaneously felt sorrowful compassion for this monk.
At that time, as the king was lying down, he dreamed that a celestial being came and said to him:
"If you wish to cure this bhikṣu of Zhichengyi’s illness, you must obtain the flesh and blood of a living person to drink and eat; then he will be healed."
The king awoke, trembling with alarm and finding no joy, and thought:
"This bhikṣu’s illness is grave; he requires that medicine, which is difficult to obtain according to the Dharma."
The King issued an edict to ask his ministers:
"From where can human flesh and blood be obtained?
At that time, the King’s eldest crown prince—named Jīvala (translated into Chinese as Zhìzhǐ, meaning "Wisdom-Stopping")—addressed the King:
"O King, do not grieve, do not lament, and do not be distressed!
Human flesh and blood are most base and insignificant; that which the people of the world value does not contradict the Way."
The king replied to the prince,
"Excellent, excellent! The prince remained silent,
returned to his meditation chamber, took a knife and cut his own thigh, taking the flesh and blood to deliver them to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu was able to take it, and his wound was immediately healed, his body attaining peace and comfort.

When the king heard that the bhikṣu had been cured, he was filled with great joy and delight, so profound that he could not contain himself; his mind remained fixed on the bhikṣu, no longer thinking of the prince’s pain. With this shared joy, they each possessed a sincere heart.
The prince also recovered his health, whereupon the king bestowed all the wealth and treasures of the nation upon him.
The Crown Prince answered the King with a verse:

“By bestowing flesh and blood for the sake of peace and security, and by cutting off flesh and blood to give to others, one immediately attains healing and is no longer afraid; this is the offering praised by the Buddha.”
Among all virtues, this virtue is the most peaceful; he who shall become a Buddha in the future has severed lust and abandoned anger, bringing healing to all people.
The Buddha told the youth Candraprabha:
"At that time, the bhikṣu Sārthavāha was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
at that time, King Jñānabala was the present Bodhisattva Maitreya."
At that time, I was Prince Jñānasthita.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has brought immeasurable benefit to the world; because he has accumulated merit with the desire to deliver all beings, the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are all like this.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to seek deliverance from the suffering of the world, they should resolve their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and recite and practice this samādhi.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
Thus ends the *Moon-Light Bodhisattva Sutra* preached by the Buddha.
